text: About fifteen drones were reported over the camp in eastern Belgium during the night. This is the first case in the federal prosecutor's file. Origin unknown; the investigation was still open in April 2026.
title: Elsenborn army camp

text: CS
st: The arrests and the finds are confirmed; the plot itself is suspected until a court rules.
title: Police arrested three young men suspected of preparing an attack on Prime Minister Bart De Wever with a home-made explosive carried by a drone. A home-made explosive and a 3D printer were found. The federal prosecutor called it jihadist-inspired, so this is terrorism, not a foreign state. One suspect was released; the lawyers of the two others deny any attack plan. No verdict found.
cat: Antwerp: plot with an explosive drone

text: RK
st: The sightings are reported; the link to Russia is a claim by the minister.
title: Drones were reported over the base on several nights. Defence Minister Theo Francken called it "a clear mission targeting Kleine-Brogel" and pointed at Russia. No evidence for that has been made public.

text: CS
st: The closure and the cancelled flights are confirmed; that real drones caused it is suspected. A later VRT fact-check found that some of the footage showed helicopters and a plane.
title: Both airports stopped air traffic in the evening after drone reports. Brussels Airport counted 81 cancelled and 24 diverted flights. This is the day the Crisis Centre gives as the first of the wave.

text: The government decided to make the National Air Security Centre in Beauvechain (Bevekom) fully operational by 1 January 2026, staffed around the clock by Defence, police, customs and aviation services, and agreed in principle to an emergency plan of €50 million for detection, jammers and drone guns. Anti-drone teams from Germany, the United Kingdom and France came to help.
title: National Security Council

text: CS
st: The stop is confirmed; the drone is suspected.
title: Flights were halted again for a short time after a new drone report.

text: Five drones were reported over the plant in the evening. The plant kept running; no danger to the reactors was reported.
title: Doel nuclear plant

text: Brussels and Liège airports stopped air traffic nine times in all: seven times in November, twice in December (Interior Minister Quintin in parliament).
title: Airports

text: C
st: The number of reports is confirmed. A report is not a confirmed drone.
title: The National Crisis Centre had logged 558 reports of suspicious drones since September 2025: 130 over military sites and 66 over nuclear sites. The minister added that the total may be too high, and that some flights may never have been reported.

text: CN
st: The findings of the broadcaster are on record; hostile drones are not proven.
title: The programme found no confirmed evidence that hostile drones flew over Belgium in late 2025. In several cases the "drones" were police helicopters or ordinary aircraft. The federal prosecutor said 26 investigations into about 40 incidents were still open and drew no conclusion. Some security sources kept saying they had little doubt about Russia, without evidence being shown.

text: The Brussels prosecutor opened an investigation into the emergency purchase of anti-drone equipment, bought without competition and against a negative advice. The federal audit service declined to look into it (May). A parliamentary committee asked the Court of Audit for an audit (June). On 16 September the prosecutor closed the case: no criminal offence. The audit question is still open.
title: The €50 million purchase

text: CS
st: The arrest is confirmed; the offence is suspected until a court rules.
title: A 46-year-old man was arrested in an investigation led by military intelligence, suspected of passing state secrets to people linked to Russia. Reported as the first Belgian arrest of this kind. Officials speak of "disposable agents": low-paid people recruited online for single jobs. What was leaked is not public.

text: A drone was seen on a Friday evening around 21:45, by eye and on radar according to air traffic control. Landings stopped for about 25 minutes and three flights were diverted (two to Ostend, one to Liège). A second sighting the next evening had little effect. Type and pilot unknown. The date comes from secondary reports.
title: Brussels Airport

text: After a National Security Council on hybrid threats, General Frederik Vansina said there was no concrete threat against Belgium at that moment, while Belgium and Europe are strengthening themselves.
title: Chief of Defence

text: SK
st: Suspected and claimed, by several sides at once; no Belgian attribution.
title: Who is behind the attacks on supermarket freezers is disputed. France accuses Iran's Revolutionary Guard for the attack of 11–12 October on more than 700 French sites, and Paris prosecutors issued international arrest warrants. In Belgium the interior minister says there are "enough elements" that Iran is very probably behind it; the foreign minister and the federal prosecutor say that cannot be confirmed at this stage. Pro-Russian groups (NoName057(16), Z-Pentest) claimed the attacks; Russia denies. See the page on the freezer attacks.

text: False bomb threats hit more than 27 flights in a Europe-wide wave. Nobody has been named.
title: Hoax bomb threats

text: Three attacks that flood a website with traffic until it goes down. The website was unreachable for four hours in total. The water supply itself was not affected. From the company's own annual report.
title: Vivaqua (Brussels)

text: The company reports phishing attempts every day and says phishing and other attacks are rising, pointing at the geopolitical situation. No number given.
title: Vivaqua (Brussels)

text: Warned customers about fake emails and text messages that abuse its planned merger of services with Farys under the name Waterunie. This is fraud against customers, not an attack on the water system.
title: De Watergroep (Flanders)

text: New fake messages: "submit your meter reading" and a promised refund of €124. Fraud against customers.
title: Farys and the town of Zelzate

text: Reported many fake emails in the name of De Watergroep or Waterunie. Fraud against customers.
title: Aquaduin (Koksijde)

text: Says the threat continues in 2026 and that it has strengthened its security to spot threats earlier (VRT).
title: Vivaqua

text: The EU cyber agency ENISA ranks drinking water and waste water among the least mature of all the sectors it assessed; waste water is the weaker of the two.
title: The sector in Europe

text: CN
st: The freezer attacks are confirmed; a link to Belgian water is not proven.
title: The freezer attacks reached Belgium: small industrial controllers that were reachable from the internet. Water plants use the same kind of controllers. No Belgian water company has been reported hit, and one Belgian report says explicitly that the freezer incidents do not show a threat to drinking water.
cat: Not water, but the same kind of equipment

text: A cyberattack on the port was reported. No details on impact found.
title: Port of Ostend

text: Ransomware; core operations were not disrupted.
title: bpost

text: Ransomware hit the check-in and boarding software that many airlines share. Staff went back to pen and paper. On Sunday 21 September 44 to 50 departures were cancelled; for Monday the airport asked airlines to cancel half of all departures (nearly 140); by Wednesday the cut was down to 10%. Disruption lasted until 28 September. The EU cyber agency confirmed it was ransomware at a supplier. British police arrested a man in West Sussex and released him on bail; no charge found.
title: Brussels Airport, through its supplier Collins Aerospace

text: Air traffic stopped nine times after drone reports. No drone was ever proven. See the page on drones and hybrid threats.
title: Brussels and Liège airports

text: Police held 11 people (5 remanded) for smuggling at least 495 kg of cocaine through the port in shipments of bananas and second-hand cars. Investigators found the gang had earlier tried to break into the computer system of an Antwerp freight forwarder. It failed, partly because the firm was about to change systems. The prosecutor called such an attempt "rather exceptional".
title: Port of Antwerp: a drug gang that also tried hacking

text: The Amsterdam appeal court sentenced a 44-year-old man to seven years for breaking into port systems in Rotterdam, Barendrecht and Antwerp between September 2020 and April 2021, so that cocaine could pass unnoticed. In Antwerp a terminal employee plugged in a USB stick with malware for him. The crime is older; the verdict falls in this period.
title: Hacker of port systems: seven years

text: Port employees in sensitive jobs are screened by the federal police and security services. A news agency headline speaks of hundreds suspended; no official number found. Unions call the screening too strict.
title: Port of Antwerp: staff screening

text: Customs intercepted 55 tonnes of cocaine in the port of Antwerp in 2025.
title: Customs figure

text: The government approved a separate prosecutor's office against organised drug crime in the Antwerp port area, with money from 2027. In the previous year Belgian courts handled 80 cases of drug imports through Antwerp: 242 convictions, 918 years of prison.
title: A prosecutor's office for the port

text: A campaign to protect port staff against approaches by criminals.
title: PortAware

text: An attack from 29 July hit at least eight European warehouses of this logistics group and exposed customer data of web shops. The reports do not say whether a Belgian warehouse was among them.
title: CEVA Logistics

text: A drone seen by eye and on radar: landings stopped for about 25 minutes, three flights diverted. Operator unknown.
title: Brussels Airport

text: A computer problem left train information and the journey planner out of date. Infrabel said it was not a hack and had no effect on safety or punctuality.
title: Infrabel

text: A LOT flight from Warsaw was searched on landing in Brussels and a Ryanair flight to Charleroi was affected, in the Europe-wide wave. All false; nobody named.
title: Hoax bomb threats

text: Dozens of aircraft over Belgium, the Netherlands, eastern England and north-west Germany lost their satellite positioning signal. Experts place the source at sea north of Texel and suspect deliberate jamming from a ship. Russian ships were in the North Sea at the time; that link is speculation.
title: Satellite navigation disturbed

text: The Danish shipping company confirmed a break-in to an older system; a ransomware group demands $5 million. No effect on Antwerp found.
title: Maersk

text: Belgian police raided more than 20 addresses and sealed two offices inside the European Parliament in an investigation into bribes paid by lobbyists for the Chinese company Huawei. Four people were charged with bribery and membership of a criminal organisation, a fifth with money laundering. Huawei lobbyists were banned from the Parliament.
title: Huawei and the European Parliament

text: Fake videos of Prime Minister Bart De Wever promise viewers quick money through an investment platform; fake Le Soir articles go with them. Fact-checkers traced it to fraudsters. In May a deepfake also used the Flemish minister-president.
title: Deepfake of the prime minister

text: A new fake video uses real footage of a 2024 interview with a forged voice of the prime minister; another fake advert adds a well-known VRT journalist.
title: More deepfakes

text: Three young men were arrested in Antwerp; the federal prosecutor called the plot jihadist-inspired. See the page on drones and sabotage.
title: Drone plot against the prime minister

text: Fake Facebook profiles of Vlaams Belang and N-VA politicians lured followers into WhatsApp groups with "exclusive news" and investment advice.
title: Fake party profiles

text: The pro-Russian group NoName057(16) aimed 57.3% of all its attacks that week at Belgium, by a security firm's count.
title: Provinces and towns knocked offline

text: The Guardian, quoting European intelligence and security officials, reported a Russian intimidation campaign against Belgian politicians and the bosses of Euroclear, the Brussels firm that holds about €185 billion of frozen Russian assets. The sources believe Russian military intelligence is behind it but disagree on how serious the threat is. The prime minister's spokesman would not comment, for safety reasons.
title: Intimidation over the frozen Russian money

text: Bart De Wever said publicly: "Moscow has let us know that in the event of a seizure, Belgium and I personally will feel the effects for eternity."
title: The prime minister's own words

text: Belgium's new Penal Code, voted in February 2024, replaces the code of 1867 and comes into force in 2026. Spying and foreign interference are punishable in peacetime, and secretly influencing democratic processes to harm national interests counts as interference. The exact date of entry into force was not verified.
title: Spying and foreign interference become crimes

text: The government approved a draft agreement to develop a new electronic voting system that works offline. The present voting computers have been in use since 2012 and the supplier's contract ends in January 2027. Background: in June 2024 at least 2,171 voters were given the wrong ballots.
title: A new voting system

text: A chip researcher held since May for allegedly sending secrets to a Chinese copy of his company; a Canadian former NATO intern arrested in July, suspected of spying for China; a Chinese national arrested in September over chip secrets. From press reports; investigations continue.
title: Three cases linked to China

text: A 46-year-old man was arrested. See the page on drones and sabotage.
title: State secrets to people linked to Russia

text: The European Parliament lifted the immunity of one Italian member (344 for, 234 against, 25 abstentions) and kept it for the others whom Belgian prosecutors had asked about; reports differ on whether that is three or four. He denies wrongdoing. By September one outlet called the investigation stalled, with about 15 current and former members drawn in.
title: Immunity vote in the Huawei case

text: Researchers at Citizen Lab found that the iPhone of a former Greek member of the European Parliament was infected at least three times with the spyware Pegasus in 2022 and 2023, while he sat on the Parliament's own committee investigating spyware. The Parliament says a detection service has been open to all members since 2022. Belgian member Saskia Bricmont called for binding rules. No state has been named.
title: Pegasus on the phone of a member of the spyware inquiry

text: The profiles of Sander Loones and Siegfried Bracke were taken over by crypto fraudsters, who posted forged photos of expensive cars supposedly bought with crypto profits.
title: X accounts of two Flemish politicians hijacked

text: Two related campaigns by the pro-Russian group NoName057(16) hit telecom, health and intelligence websites.
title: Health websites knocked offline

text: Ransomware. The hospital switched off every server as a precaution. Operations were cancelled, about 70 patients were sent home and seven in critical care were moved to other hospitals; it ran at about half capacity and worked on paper. The hospital says it paid no ransom and that, as far as it knows, no patient data was stolen. The federal computer crime unit and the national cyber team investigated; nobody has been named.
title: AZ Monica, Antwerp and Deurne

text: One report quotes the prosecutor saying no ransom was demanded; others describe it as ransomware with a demand. Not settled in the sources found.
title: Was a ransom demanded?

text: A report by the hospitals' shared security platform SHIELD and the federal health ministry, based on measurements in more than fifty hospitals: three in four must take urgent extra steps to reach the required level. Smaller and psychiatric hospitals lag most, for lack of money and specialists; Flemish hospitals score better on average than Walloon and Brussels ones. The government has put in €105 million since 2022, of which €40 million in 2024.
title: The government's own measurement

text: After AZ Monica a security firm found that a supplier of patient-registration software used by AZ Monica also served other hospitals, and that passwords for their platforms were circulating. Its testers could reach the data of about 71,000 patients; one report says the details of at least five hospitals were found on the dark web. The firm warned the national cyber centre and the hospitals; the holes were closed. It saw no sign that criminals had taken the patient files. The hospitals were not named.
title: 71,000 patient records within reach

text: Medication, imaging, emergency systems and the website worked again after about five weeks; visitor wifi stayed off. The prosecutor's investigation was still open.
title: AZ Monica back

text: The Qilin ransomware group listed the clinic and threatened to publish patient data. A Belgian blog says Qilin claimed two Belgian health targets within 24 hours; the second is not named. No confirmation by the clinic found.
title: Louise Medical Center, Brussels

text: Ransomware at ChipSoft on 7 April forced Dutch hospitals to close patient portals. Early reports said Belgian hospitals were affected too, and VRT reported on the Antwerp hospital group ZAS, a customer. On 16 April ChipSoft said no Belgian care institution was hit and that data was taken only at a few Dutch ones; on 29 April it said experts confirmed the stolen data was destroyed.
title: ChipSoft, the Dutch maker of hospital record software

text: As "essential entities" under the cybersecurity law, hospitals had to show by this date that they meet the required level or have a plan; late or incomplete files can bring fines. How hospitals did is not published in the sources found.
title: Deadline for hospitals

text: A seller claimed to have data from the medical-practice platform cabinetmedical.be; another offered a database said to belong to the health insurance fund Christelijke Mutualiteit. Neither was independently verified.
title: Two unverified offers on criminal forums

text: Belgium set up a Cyber Command inside Defence, now called the Belgian Cyber Force. It sits close to military intelligence and deals with threats from abroad; the civilian Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB) leads national policy.
title: Background: a cyber branch of the army

text: The government agreed a defence plan of about €34 billion in investments up to 2034. It includes cyber, electronic warfare, drones and counter-drones, and air defence. A trade report puts half a billion euros on cybersecurity projects up to 2034 and €965 million on military data centres, inside a €1.6 billion package for digital resilience.
title: The Strategic Vision

text: Major General Pierre Ciparisse has led the Cyber Force since the summer of 2025. He calls staff the first priority and gives no headcount.
title: New commander

text: The pro-Russian group NoName057(16) claimed an attack on several websites of the military intelligence service. Defence said the sites were briefly unreachable, nothing was broken into and no data leaked.
title: Military intelligence websites knocked offline

text: The Cyber Force ran a public challenge to attract cyber reservists.
title: A competition to find reservists

text: About €50 million of anti-drone equipment and a strengthened air security centre, after the drone reports. See the page on drones and sabotage.
title: Emergency purchases

text: Defence chose Proximus NXT as its strategic partner for cyber defence.
title: A telecom firm as strategic partner

text: 32% of the Cyber Force's staff were civilians in February 2026. In an interview the commander gave a mix of 47% military, 25% reservists and the rest civilians; the two figures come from different moments.
title: Who works there

text: The defence minister publicly asked cyber specialists to join the Cyber Force as reserve officers.
title: A call to experts

text: The operations plan for 2026, approved by the government, says the Cyber Force supports the competent authorities with monitoring and threat analysis, and that Defence's Cyber Rapid Response Teams stand ready for serious national cyber incidents.
title: What the army may do at home

text: Belgium reported 3.44% of its economy spent on defence and security: 2.01% on the military and, counted for the first time, 1.43% on "strategic resilience" (cybersecurity, counter-terrorism, vital infrastructure). For 2026 the defence budget is €10.6 billion.
title: The NATO count

text: Attackers used flaws in phone-management software (Ivanti) at an outside partner to reach personal data of staff of State Security; disclosed in June 2026. Classified data stayed safe; nobody has been named.
title: The civilian intelligence service, not the army

text: A man suspected of passing state secrets to people linked to Russia. See the page on drones and sabotage.
title: An arrest led by military intelligence

text: The government approved a contract for advanced digital training and certificates for the cyber branch.
title: Training bought in

text: Belgium will keep military spending at 2% of the economy until 2029; a path towards NATO's 3.5% goal still has to be drawn up.
title: The next years

text: The Balticconnector gas pipeline and two telecom cables were damaged. Background: before this file’s two years, and the start of the series.
title: Finland–Estonia

text: Two data cables cut within a day of each other. European ministers spoke of hybrid warfare. Background.
title: Sweden–Lithuania and Finland–Germany

text: A power cable and several data cables damaged. Finland boarded and held the ship. See the courts and the hybrid page: the case was thrown out for lack of jurisdiction in October 2025 and revived on appeal in August 2026.
title: Finland–Estonia, the tanker Eagle S

text: Sweden seized the ship on suspicion of sabotage, then released it: prosecutors concluded the damage came from weather, poor equipment and poor seamanship. The clearest case of an alarm that was not an attack.
title: Latvia–Gotland, the ship Vezhen

text: A data cable damaged; sabotage suspected. No outcome found.
title: Germany–Finland

text: A standing patrol of the Baltic to watch over cables and pipelines. A secondary source quotes NATO as saying sabotage fell sharply in its first year and that response times went from 17 hours to one; the primary document was not found.
title: NATO starts Baltic Sentry

text: Finnish special forces boarded the ship; a drag mark about 10 km long was found on the seabed. On 5 November 2026 a Helsinki court sentenced the Russian captain to three and a half years and an Azerbaijani crew member to two years and ten months for aggravated sabotage. The first prison sentences in Europe for cutting sea cables.
title: Finland–Estonia, the ship Fitburg

text: A fibre cable failed; NATO and police investigated. No outcome found.
title: Latvia–Gotland again

country: Thirteen countries and Iceland speak together
text: A joint statement on growing interference with satellite navigation for shipping in the Baltic and the North Sea.
title: Thirteen countries and Iceland speak together

text: Flights meeting satellite-navigation interference rose from about 200 a day in early 2024 to about 900 a day by the second quarter, on a secondary count. Lithuania says transmitters in Kaliningrad can falsify signals up to 450 km away, which covers much of Poland, the Baltic states and part of the Nordic countries.
title: Jamming becomes normal

country: The air safety agency raises the alarm again
text: EASA issued the fourth revision of its safety bulletin on satellite-navigation outages, saying incidents are becoming more severe, more sophisticated and more disruptive. Its worst-affected list for mid-July 2026 included Tallinn, Riga, Helsinki, Vilnius and Warsaw, alongside Ankara and Istanbul.
title: The air safety agency raises the alarm again

text: A Danish technical university study found that the jamming over Europe also disturbs the position-finding of satellites in low orbit as they pass over.
title: It reaches space

text: About 80 aircraft over north-west Europe, including planes approaching Amsterdam, lost or lost confidence in their satellite position. Seven of them had navigation trouble on approach to Schiphol. Dutch air traffic control calls deliberate jamming a plausible explanation and says safety was not compromised; the Dutch investigation is still open and no official finding exists. A data analyst places the source 80 to 110 nautical miles north of Texel, where six Russian-flagged ships were sailing; shipping news sites say three of them are on the EU sanctions list for carrying weapons. Belgium’s own air traffic service told VRT it received no reports of jamming or spoofing that day.
title: The North Sea

text: Ransomware at the secondary school OLV Pulhof in Berchem, Antwerp, shortly after the Christmas holiday. The attackers said they had been inside the systems unnoticed for more than a year and claimed 45 GB of data, including identity cards, diplomas and mental-health records. They asked for about €100,000, then about €15,000. The school refused. The attackers then emailed the parents directly, asking €50 per child. Experts said that email probably did not come from the group it claimed to be. Belgian prosecutors are investigating.
title: A school, and then its parents

text: A breach of the learning platform Canvas reached VUB, Thomas More, Artevelde, Karel de Grote, Erasmushogeschool and CVO Gent: names, email addresses and student numbers of thousands of people. Icelandic universities were named in the same breach.
title: Six colleges and universities at once

text: A ransomware group claimed 21 GB of data from schools in Styria. The education authority refused to negotiate and the outage was repaired quickly.
title: Schools in Styria

text: A criminal claimed about 43 GB covering millions of pupils and staff. Not verified, and no ministry confirmation was found.
title: The education ministry

text: La Sapienza in Rome was forced offline; the Interlock group claimed it and published the data after no ransom was paid.
title: A university offline for days

text: A commercial tracker counted 104 attacks on education in six months: 36 confirmed and 68 claimed but unconfirmed. The median ransom asked was about $420,000.
title: What the trackers count

text: Education went from 1 recorded incident in 2025 to 45 in 2026. Most of that is better reporting rather than a forty-fold rise; see the register.
title: In this file’s own register

text: The Commission proposed the EU KIDS Act: no social media under 13, safety built into platforms and games by design, age checks certified by the EU using technology that proves an age without revealing who you are, and fines up to 6% of worldwide turnover. Comments were open until 3 December 2026.
title: A law aimed at children, not at schools

text: France passed a law barring under-15s from social media on 21 July 2026. The Constitutional Council blocked it on 14 August 2026.
title: A national ban struck down

text: The Commission put Austria’s draft ban for under-14s on hold, as it has done with other national rules, while its own proposal is on the table.
title: Brussels pauses a national law

text: Holding the EU presidency, Denmark wants a hard ban under 13 and parental consent from 13 to 15. One source gives its own national plan as under 15.
title: Denmark pushes from the chair

text: In the "chat control" talks the negotiators agreed that that regulation is not the place to regulate age verification, which is why it now sits in the KIDS Act instead. See encryption.
title: Age checks taken out of the other law

text: Australia became the first country to ban social media for under-16s.
title: The example everyone quotes

text: A Vienna court convicted former intelligence officer Egisto Ott of spying for Russia: four years and one month. He passed information to Russian services and to the fugitive Jan Marsalek, including a secure government laptop for €20,000. He has appealed.
Explosion and fire at an ammunition warehouse of the arms maker EMCO, which supplies Ukraine. The interior minister first pointed away from outside causes.
A drone exploded near the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline. One source; no official finding.
A second fire at another EMCO depot near Tsareva Livada, 33 days later. Nobody hurt. The minister said sabotage is one of the lines of inquiry and ordered every ammunition depot inspected.
The state news agency reported that prosecutors see a link between four ammunition-warehouse blasts and suspect Russia. Russia rejects this.

Drones hit two commercial ships in Bulgaria's economic zone at sea, a first. On 13 October the HS Dignity was struck; 11 sailors missing, five survivors (Bloomberg). The prime minister summoned the Russian ambassador; Bulgaria has not formally blamed Russia.
One news round-up mentions an arson investigation near Omiš taking a terrorism angle. Not confirmed in a primary source.

Drones hit the British base RAF Akrotiri on the island, damaging a hangar. Cypriot officials said they were launched from Lebanon, probably by Hezbollah, during the Iran war. Not a Russian case. Greece and France sent jets, frigates and anti-drone systems.
A Prague court sentenced a Colombian man to eight years for an arson attack and for planning another; the case is believed to be possibly linked to Russia.

Arson at a warehouse of the defence firm LPP Holding in Pardubice. Suspects were held in Czechia, Slovakia and later Bulgaria on terrorism charges. A group claimed it over the firm's Israeli ties; Czech intelligence asked publicly whether Russia used that group as cover.
Prague airport was among the worst hit by the Europe-wide hoax bomb threats: nine flights on one day.

Copenhagen Airport closed for about four hours after reports of two or three large drones; at least 35 incoming flights were diverted. Police did not shoot, because of the fuel depots and the full aircraft nearby. On 23 September Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called it "the most serious attack on Danish critical infrastructure to date" and said she could not rule out Russia. Nobody was named.
61 reports of drones over Aalborg and military sites in Jutland.
The police district reviewed those 61 reports: no evidence of illegal drone flights that concern security. It withdrew its earlier word "verified".
Police closed the nine-month Copenhagen investigation: no evidence that the flying objects were drones, although drone activity "cannot be ruled out". No suspects.

Arson at a supermarket in Osula and later at a Ukrainian restaurant in Tallinn. A court sentenced a man to six and a half years and said it was ordered by Russian military intelligence. Date of the verdict not found.
The cargo ship Fitburg dragged its anchor about 130 km and damaged cables, partly in Estonia's zone. See Finland for the verdict.
Arson at a Tallinn building used by Milrem Robotics, which makes military robots. Three Latvian suspects were detained in Latvia and handed over.
The Estonian government and its security service formally said the Milrem arson was "commissioned by Russian security services". The Kremlin denies it.
Eagle S (cables cut in December 2024): the Helsinki court dismissed the case, saying Finland had no jurisdiction.
The Fitburg damaged undersea cables between Finland and Estonia.
The appeal court reversed the Eagle S ruling: Finland does have jurisdiction, because the damage was felt there. The case goes back to the lower court; the three accused have left the country.

Fitburg: the Russian captain got three and a half years and an Azerbaijani crew member two years and ten months for aggravated sabotage. The court found they acted on purpose. The captain will appeal. The reports found do not say who, if anyone, ordered it.

Nine pig heads were left outside mosques around Paris. Three Serbs were later convicted in Serbia (house arrest) for acts in France and Germany; Serbia's interior ministry said the group was trained by a man acting for a foreign intelligence service. No state was named by a court.
Four Russian men were arrested on suspicion of plotting to kill the Russian dissident Vladimir Osechkin, who lives in France.
A research count (ICCT/GLOBSEC) puts France second in Europe with 20 Russia-linked incidents since 2022.

French investigators were reported to be working on several suspected Russia-linked cases, among them railway infrastructure and a Belarus-born man held near Toulouse after filming a military drone prototype.

Freezer controls at more than 700 supermarket sites were attacked (a cyber case, listed here because of who is blamed). French authorities suspect Iran's Revolutionary Guard; Paris prosecutors issued international arrest warrants. Pro-Russian groups also claimed it.
Paris prosecutors are examining whether foreign powers are behind the hoax bomb threats against flights.
Munich Airport closed twice in 24 hours after drone reports.
The federal police chief counted more than 1,000 suspicious drone flights. One Frankfurt shutdown turned out to be a 41-year-old hobby pilot testing a new drone.
Fire on the rail line between Düsseldorf and Cologne damaged signal cables; investigated as possible sabotage. No link to any state found.
Leipzig/Halle Airport: a drone carrying explosives was found near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane; the charge did not go off. Three drones were found in all. Reports differ on details.
A drone forced repeated closures at Hanover Airport; federal police could not stop it with their equipment (Der Spiegel).

The German government formally blamed Russia for the Leipzig attack ("police investigations, patterns of the act and intelligence findings") and ordered the Russian consulate general in Bonn closed. Russia called it absurd. No arrests found.
A confidential police report, cited by Süddeutsche Zeitung, counts more than 165 suspected acts of sabotage and nearly 750 suspicious drone incidents since January 2026.
Two Belarusian men were arrested in southern Germany, suspected of planning fires near a railway line and a power line for Russia. Romania links them to the Brașov fire.

After the Leipzig case the new government called Russian hybrid activity a serious threat. One outlet notes that no sabotage incidents have been recorded in Hungary; not checked against official data.

Four or five military-style drones appeared near Dublin Airport shortly after President Zelensky's plane landed. The prime minister called it "suggestive" of a Russian-inspired hybrid campaign; the Russian embassy called that baseless. Police are still looking at whether they took off from land or from a ship; no evidence against three sanctioned ships nearby. The navy had no means to stop them.

On the first full day of the Winter Olympics, cables were cut near Bologna, a crude explosive device was found by a track and a switch burned near Pesaro; delays of up to two and a half hours. Nobody claimed it; investigators looked at anarchist groups. No state link reported.
Two people were convicted at first instance for mapping ports and barracks for Russia.
Two former intelligence agents were arrested in Rome for selling classified information to a Russian agent with diplomatic cover; five others, four of them soldiers, are under investigation.
More than 6,000 schools received threats in the week of the hoax bomb threats against flights. One source; nobody named.
A data cable between Latvia and Gotland was damaged. See Sweden: prosecutors found it was not sabotage.
Four arson attacks on railway sites in Riga. Two people received prison sentences in September 2026 for acting on Russia's behalf.
A drone came down in the Krāslava district; identified as Ukrainian, flying in from Russia.

Two drones crashed in Latvia; one set an oil depot in Rēzekne on fire. The army identified them as Ukrainian drones aimed at Russia that strayed. The defence minister was dismissed and the government fell within a week.
A Riga court sentenced an electrician to five and a half years for spying for Russian military intelligence.

Balloons carrying smuggled cigarettes from Belarus have closed Vilnius Airport again and again: more than 20 times by one count. Lithuania closed the border from 29 October to 19 November 2025 and declared a state of emergency on 9 December 2025. It blames Belarus for letting it happen and calls it a hybrid attack.
A Vilnius court sentenced a young Ukrainian to three years and four months for the 2024 arson at IKEA and an attempted attack in Šiauliai, carried out for Russian military intelligence.
Italian jets on NATO air policing shot down a drone near Pratkūnai. Officials said it most likely came from Belarus and was likely carrying explosives.
Vilnius Airport closed again for more than three hours because of balloons.
Findel airport closed for just over three hours after unidentified drones were seen: 19 aircraft diverted, more than 1,800 passengers affected (government statement).
A second closure of about 52 minutes; sources differ on the day. No operator, motive or state link identified; investigation open, no suspects.
The freezer attacks also hit Luxembourg. France blames Iran for its own wave; no finding for Luxembourg found.
Drones were reported over Volkel air base and Eindhoven; soldiers fired at them, and Eindhoven Airport stopped traffic on 22 November. A research institute counted nine incidents.
The investigation produced no suspects and no recovered drone.
A British think tank (IISS) said the drones were probably launched from ships of the Russian "shadow fleet". Dutch authorities have not named anyone; Russia denies it.
Oslo Airport was disrupted by drone reports. Police found no evidence of the drones.
The security service PST: not one case in 2025 of a drone flown by a foreign power; many reports were not drones at all.

PST raised its warning: it expects Russian intelligence to try sabotage in Norway in the coming year, most likely against defence firms. It has found no sabotage attempts so far, but Russia-linked actors have mapped targets.

About 19 drones crossed into Poland during a Russian attack on Ukraine; three or four were shot down, the first time a NATO member fired in this war. A house in Wyryki-Wola was destroyed by debris; nobody hurt. Poland invoked NATO's Article 4. Moscow denied responsibility.
Eight people detained over suspected Russia-linked sabotage. At least 44 had been detained for spying or sabotage since 2022 (count of August 2025).

An explosive device damaged the Warsaw–Lublin railway near Mika; the next day a train with 475 passengers braked hard near Puławy. Nobody hurt. The government called both sabotage by Russian intelligence. Two Ukrainian suspects fled to Belarus.
A Russian man was charged with directing a sabotage ring from the Moscow region.
A research count (ICCT/GLOBSEC) puts Poland first in Europe: 31 of 151 Russia-linked incidents since 2022.
Two Ukrainian men were detained for photographing infrastructure and military sites and for car arson, paid partly in cryptocurrency.
A third man was indicted for helping prepare the Mika attack; the sabotage charge carries ten years to life. No conviction yet.
The Iberian blackout hit Portugal too. Officials found no sign of a cyberattack or sabotage.
A drone entered Romanian airspace during a Russian attack on Ukraine; fragments have fallen on Romanian soil repeatedly since 2022.
A Russian drone reportedly hit an apartment building in Galați, injuring two. One source.
Fire at the Carfil industrial site in Brașov, next to a state arms maker; the arms production itself was not damaged.

Drones struck commercial ships off Romania. A grain ship sank on 5 October about 30 nautical miles out, two crew killed. The Khoryv sank on 23 October off Constanța, one dead and three missing; the president said a Russian drone did it. Bloomberg counts seven ships hit off Romania and Bulgaria and more than two dozen sailors killed, the first deaths from drones inside EU waters.

The intelligence service said a Russia-coordinated network was behind the Brașov fire. Three suspects (two Belarusians, one Ukrainian) are under investigation; reports differ on whether they are in custody. Russia denies it.

Police said they foiled an arson attack on the Skyeton drone factory near Prešov: two suspects held in Slovakia, one in Germany. A Latvian suspect said he was hired through Telegram by a Russian speaker. The Russian embassy denied any role.

German investigators were reported to link the Skyeton plot, an arson in Munich and the Leipzig drone to Russian military intelligence, with part of the network working from Slovakia. Media reports, not a charge.
The Iberian blackout: officials and a later report found no cyberattack.
Copper cable was stolen at five points on the Madrid–Seville high-speed line, stopping trains. The transport minister called it "serious sabotage". No link to any state found.
Spain led a Europol operation against a network that recruited saboteurs remotely; two central figures live in Russia.
The foreign minister called the hoax bomb threats most likely "an attempt at hybrid aggression". Nobody has been named.

A data cable between Latvia and Gotland was damaged; Sweden seized the ship Vezhen on suspicion of sabotage. Prosecutors then concluded it was weather, poor equipment and poor seamanship: not sabotage.
Drones were reported over the Karlskrona archipelago, near the main naval base. Police said it was unclear what the object was.
Gothenburg-Landvetter Airport stopped traffic after drone reports; police opened an investigation for aviation sabotage. Outcome not found.
Several drones were reported over strategically important sites in canton Aargau.

The federal intelligence service: Russia's hybrid conflict "is becoming more aggressive and hits Switzerland directly". It identified "disposable agents" with links to Switzerland and says Russia misuses Swiss computer systems for sabotage abroad. No arrests in Switzerland found.

Attackers changed the water pressure at the Tureby Alkestrup waterworks near Køge; at least three pipes burst and homes were left without water. The head of the waterworks said it happened after a switch to cheaper, weaker security.

The Danish Defence Intelligence Service publicly blamed Russia: the attack was carried out by the pro-Russian group Z-Pentest, which the service says the Russian state uses as an instrument. Denmark summoned the Russian ambassador. Denmark's first public attribution of this kind.
The municipal utilities of Kamen, Bönen and Bergkamen were attacked; the customer portal and direct debits failed, the supply did not.

Only water suppliers serving 500,000 people or more fall under the German rules for critical infrastructure; most are below that line. No case found of attackers taking over the controls of a German water plant.

The intelligence service warned that Dutch water and power companies had been targeted; an official said Russia is "embedding itself" in vital sectors so it can disrupt them later. No disruption so far.

Attackers opened a valve at a dam in Bremanger and let about 500 litres of water per second run for four hours before it was noticed. No damage. The way in was a weak password on a control panel reachable from the internet.
The head of the security service attributed it to pro-Russian hackers. The Russian embassy called that unfounded. One legal study notes that no formal written attribution has been published.

Attackers got into the control systems of five water treatment plants: Jabłonna Lacka, Szczytno, Małdyty, Tolkmicko and Sierakowo. They had administrator rights and could change pump settings and alarm limits. The way in: factory passwords never changed and control systems reachable from the internet. From the security agency's report of May 2026.
Who did it: the agency's report names Russian and Belarusian state groups in general, but did not formally pin these five break-ins on them. Researchers call the attribution unconfirmed.
The deputy prime minister said an attempt to break into the water supply of a large Polish city had been stopped. The city was not named.

Ransomware hit the national water authority Apele Române: about 1,000 computer systems affected. Dams and water operations kept running. The attackers used a standard Windows encryption tool. Nobody claimed it and the authority named nobody.

Ransomware at Aigües de Mataró, which serves about 130,000 people: internal systems encrypted, customer data exposed. Supply and water quality not affected (company statement). The year is inferred; the report found gives only the day.
The public water company Acosol (Málaga) reported an attack that affected its information systems and may have exposed customer data.
The Brodosplit shipyard was hit by the Qilin ransomware group. One mention in a trade report; no date or detail found.

A new criminal group that targets logistics firms claimed it had stolen data from the freight company DSV. DSV said its operations were not disrupted and its systems were fully working; the claim later vanished from the group's site.
The shipping company Maersk confirmed that an attacker reached one older local system, inherited through an earlier takeover, and took data. A ransomware group demands $5 million.

Air France (with KLM) said customer data was taken through an outside supplier, in the week of 28 July. No payment data. Nobody named by the airlines; researchers suspect the criminal group ShinyHunters.

Software that lets an outsider control computers from a distance was found on the passenger ferry GNV Fantastic in the port of Sète. France's domestic intelligence service is investigating; a Latvian crew member was charged with acting for an unnamed foreign power. The ferry company says the attempt was stopped without consequences. Russia was mentioned in the press, not by the authorities; the suspect's lawyer disputes it.

A joint warning by American, German, Canadian, Australian and other security agencies said that unit 26165 of Russian military intelligence (also known as APT28) was attacking dozens of logistics and technology firms that move aid to Ukraine, across air, sea and rail, and had used access to private cameras near border crossings, military sites and railway stations. The warning names sectors, among them ports and airports, not individual ports; a later academic analysis named Hamburg and Rotterdam.
Berlin Brandenburg Airport was hit by the same ransomware at the check-in supplier Collins Aerospace as Brussels; average delays of about an hour were reported.

Deutsche Bahn's website and booking app were knocked offline by a flood of traffic. Information and booking worked again by 18 February. No customer data stolen. The company would not say who was behind it.

A failure of air traffic control radio grounded or disrupted flights for several hours; about 120 flights were grounded at the two largest airports. The government said a cyberattack was unlikely; a judicial inquiry was opened.
Dublin and Cork airports reported smaller effects from the Collins Aerospace ransomware. One source.
The port authority for the central Adriatic (Ancona) reported an attack, later claimed by the ransomware group Anubis. Whether terminal work was affected is unclear.
Rail sabotage near Bologna and Pesaro on the first full day of the Winter Olympics: a physical attack, described on the page about drones and sabotage.
A fault in the national data network forced air traffic control to cut capacity by up to half; full capacity was back the same day. The operator ruled out a cyberattack.
Vilnius Airport closed more than 20 times because of balloons from Belarus. See the page about drones and sabotage.
Lithuania said transmitters in Russia's Kaliningrad region can falsify satellite positioning signals up to 450 km away, covering much of Poland, the Baltic states and part of the Nordic countries.
KLM (with Air France) said customer data was taken through an outside supplier.

Eurail, the Utrecht company behind the Interrail pass, was breached: data of 308,777 people, including passport details and, for young travellers on the EU's DiscoverEU scheme, bank and health details. In February 2026 the data was offered for sale. Affected people were notified from 27 March 2026.
The Amsterdam appeal court gave a hacker seven years for breaking into port systems in Rotterdam and Antwerp in 2020–2021; about 210 kg of cocaine came in through Rotterdam with his help.
Dozens of aircraft over the Netherlands and Belgium lost their satellite positioning signal; experts place the source at sea north of Texel and suspect deliberate jamming.

Iberia said customer data was exposed through a supplier; passwords and bank details not affected. The criminal group Everest claims 596 GB and demands $6 million; the airline has not confirmed those figures.
Ransomware at the Port of Vigo: digital systems cut off, work continued by hand. A ransom was demanded; group and payment not confirmed.

The rail companies Adif and Renfe: Adif saw unusual activity on 24 September and its website went down on the 25th; Renfe said customer names and email addresses were reached through Adif's servers, and a later notice mentions identity numbers, journeys and encrypted passwords. Trains ran normally. Press figures of 500 GB and claims that the attack was run by artificial intelligence are not confirmed by either company.

Two passenger flights lost satellite navigation over the south-east, near Gotland and Öland; both landed normally on other instruments. One source. The transport agency describes continuous jamming and more organised signal-faking in the region.
The same group that named DSV listed the freight company Kuehne+Nagel as a victim. The company said only that it was aware of the mentions.

Websites knocked offline in attacks that authorities and experts attribute to pro-Russian groups; ahead of the 2026 election the government started a programme against disinformation and asked the EU for help. From a US Congress research report.
The president said he does not rule out interference by artificial intelligence in the next elections: "we are of course all vulnerable".

Parliamentary election. Researchers found networks linked to Russia trying to undermine trust in the vote, and clusters of accounts on TikTok, X and Telegram pushing foreign stories, but no operation able to change the result.
The fact-checker Demagog found hundreds of fake TikTok accounts spreading pro-Russian and anti-establishment content, and no evidence that the network was run from or by Russia.
Websites were attacked before the local elections. In December Danish military intelligence blamed the pro-Russian group NoName057(16) and linked it to the Russian state.
A Nordic fact-checking network counts 247 attacks by activist-hacker groups on Denmark in 2026; they rise around elections and decisions that go against Russia. Not tied to one election.
The state agency against foreign digital interference (Viginum) published a technical report on the Russian operation known as Storm-1516.

Before the municipal elections France accused Russia over a fake website aimed at a centre-right candidate for mayor of Paris. Viginum said it was probably the Storm-1516 network. It reached few people: under 20,000 views on X.

Viginum also found 28 Facebook pages and 15 French-language websites run from abroad that pushed alarmist AI-made content; it judged the aim to be profit, not politics. A fake audio clip of the mayor of Grenoble was made with free voice-cloning tools.
New: the agency published a weekly bulletin on foreign interference during the campaign.

Federal election, 23 February. Fake videos claimed the AfD party was missing from postal ballots; researchers counted more than 700 fake accounts in the last week. Two days before the vote the government said it had indications of a Russian campaign.

The foreign ministry: "We can now state definitively that Russia, through the Storm 1516 campaign, sought to influence and destabilise the most recent federal election." The Russian ambassador was summoned. The same day Germany blamed Russian military intelligence for the 2024 attack on air traffic control.
A deepfake of Chancellor Merz using the stolen logo of Deutsche Welle was attributed to Storm-1516. One technology outlet.
A Russian disinformation campaign was reported ahead of the state election in Saxony-Anhalt. One outlet.
TikTok removed two networks of fake accounts; a pro-Kremlin network impersonated Euronews to spread fake reports about the election.

Two Russian operations, Storm-1516 and "Matryoshka", spread fake videos, for example that Hungarian men would be drafted to fight for Ukraine if the opposition won. Analysts add that most of the disinformation in the campaign came from inside Hungary.
An attack on the app of the opposition party Tisza reportedly led to stolen data that was then passed to pro-government media. One source.
The then government declassified part of an intelligence report claiming that IT specialists close to Tisza were linked to Ukraine's volunteer hacker force. The opposition called it a fabrication.

Election day. International observers: a lively contest with record turnout, but no equal chances because of the ruling party's advantages; several AI-made videos by political actors circulated. The opposition won and formed the government.

The parliamentary committee that oversees the secret services confirmed that the government used the spyware Graphite, made by the firm Paragon, against two migration activists, and called that lawful. It found no evidence that the services targeted a journalist whose phone had also been attacked.

Researchers at Citizen Lab then confirmed with high confidence that two journalists, one of them Italian, were hit with the same spyware. Paragon ended its contracts with Italy on 9 June, saying Italy refused a check that would have settled who targeted the journalist; Italy disputes that account.

Before the election of 29 October a newspaper revealed that two members of parliament of the PVV party secretly ran a Facebook page posting hundreds of AI-made images of an opposition leader; the page had 74 million views between June and October. The party leader apologised; the opposition filed a police complaint.
An election observatory found significant digital manipulation, including new AI threats and failing moderation by platforms, and concluded the election was "tested, but fundamentally free and fair".

Parliamentary election. Websites were knocked offline; the security service linked an attack on the website of the Conservative Party to a pro-Russian hacker group. The Swedish psychological-defence agency concludes the attempts had no effect.
Prime Minister Tusk said attackers tried for about twelve hours to take over computers of his party's office and campaign staff, and spoke of foreign interference from "the east".

Days before the first round of the presidential election the state research institute NASK found political adverts on Facebook that may have been paid from abroad and that outspent every campaign committee in a week; Meta blocked them. On 16 May Tusk said Russian hackers on Telegram had knocked party websites offline.

NASK tracked more than 10,000 accounts spreading disinformation; the ministry called the Russian attempts unprecedented. Independent experts found the interference lower than expected, and international observers praised the countermeasures.

During the snap election a false story, dressed up as a CNN report, said Russian state groups had carried out a cyberattack. CNN Portugal denied it. Fact-checkers say much of the false content matched known Russian operations.
Background: the constitutional court annulled the first round of the presidential election, citing manipulation of opinion by a foreign state. Moscow denies it.
First round of the rerun. Pro-Russian hackers claimed attacks on government websites, among them the interior and justice ministries.

Run-off, won by the centrist Nicușor Dan. Telegram's founder Pavel Durov sent every Romanian user a message alleging that France had asked him to silence conservative voices; France denies it. Romanian ministries accused Russia of interfering in the run-off.
The European Commission's investigation into TikTok's handling of election risks was still running months later.

The candidate barred from the rerun, Călin Georgescu, is on trial in two cases (an attempt against the constitutional order; promoting fascist leaders), has been in pre-trial detention since 29 September and was indicted on 12 November for a €1.1 million fraud.

Parliamentary election. The pro-Russian "Matryoshka" network spread false claims of election fraud and fabricated videos against the prime minister. The psychological-defence agency said Sweden was not a priority target for Russia; the security service still ranks Russia first for interference. Voting is on paper.
The ransomware group TheGentlemen listed a fertility clinic in Wels as a victim.
The state IT company said it fought off a very large flood of traffic aimed at the national health information system.

The Ministry of Health said an attack hit some of its applications; the system with patients' medical data was not affected. The group TheGentlemen claimed the ministry and threatened to publish data.
The Bank of Cyprus Oncology Centre confirmed that patient and staff data taken from its systems was published.
Ransomware at two healthcare bodies, attributed to the Qilin group; the victims were not named.
Patient and staff data of a Czech healthcare body were offered for sale.
Hvidovre Hospital stopped ransomware on the network that runs the building's technical systems; access-card data of about 7,600 staff may have been taken. Patient care was not affected.
Patient data leaked from a chain of GP practices.
Criminals encrypted the patient data, records and appointments of a family medicine centre (national cyber agency).
A breach at Pharmadata, an IT supplier to pharmacies, was called the most serious incident of the period by the national cyber centre.
A private hospital lost the data of 524,867 patients and of 202,246 contact persons. In September 2026 the data regulator fined it €500,000 for inadequate protection of its patient-record system.
Public hospitals in the Hauts-de-France region were targeted through the servers that hold patients' identity data.

The health software company Cegedim Santé: the health minister confirmed the attack could concern more than 15 million people. The company had filed a criminal complaint in October 2025 and reportedly said nothing in public for four months.
The health-insurance payment operator Almerys confirmed a breach covering 15.4 million social security numbers.
Chaumont hospital: data lost and critical systems unavailable.
Hôpital Paris Saint-Joseph confirmed a leak covering 15,044 patients.
The university hospital of Reims confirmed that patient data was exposed through an attack on the software maker Softway Medical; how many people is not known.
The Ameos hospital group shut down all its systems after an attack; several states opened data-protection proceedings.
The district clinic in Roth (Bavaria) cut its internet link as a precaution; the emergency room closed briefly and prescriptions were written by hand.
BDH-Klinik Greifswald: the communication network was paralysed and theft of patient data was later confirmed.

A billing firm for hospitals lost the data of more than 100,000 private patients of university hospitals. In late May ransomware at a hospital group (not named) postponed operations and sent emergency patients elsewhere.
Charité Berlin: contact details of about 140,000 people.

The district hospital of Greiz-Ronneburg (Thuringia): the emergency room in Greiz could not take patients; state police and prosecutors were called in. The hospital says patient safety is not at risk.
A break-in at the Grund care home exposed data on tens of thousands of people; disclosed in February 2026. Iceland's cyber team, Europol and Interpol investigate.
The health-recruitment platform Healthdaq detected a break-in; a criminal group claims 431 GB, including CVs and identity documents.
The medical-device maker Medtronic, headquartered in Dublin: health information of 3.8 million people reportedly stolen worldwide; the company attributes it to the ShinyHunters group.
An activist-hacker group got into a hospital's camera system and published footage from operating rooms.
The public health body ASST Rhodense, which runs hospitals near Milan: stolen medical documents and prescriptions were published on the attackers' site.

A sector body counts 20% more attacks on hospitals in 2025, 47% of them ransomware. In 2026 at least four large private health facilities in Milan and Rome were reportedly hit, and the INC Ransom group listed the Policlinico Triestino (2 Sep 2026; not confirmed by the hospital).
About 62,000 records with personal data of doctors leaked from an agency of the Ministry of Health.
A major attack on a firm that hosts health data for doctors' practices was reported.

The laboratory Clinical Diagnostics, which analyses cervical-cancer screening, was hit by ransomware. The count of people affected grew from more than 405,000 women to about 941,000 people in later reports. The health inspectorate found it had not met legal security standards.

Ransomware at ChipSoft, whose patient-record software runs in 70 to 80% of Dutch hospitals. Eleven hospitals cut their links; data came from its cloud service used by GPs, rehabilitation clinics and an eye hospital. A criminal group (Embargo) claimed 100 GB; ChipSoft said on 29 April that the stolen data was destroyed. The number of patients was never disclosed.
Ransomware at the Interior Ministry hospital in Kraków and at the Bonifraterskie Medical Centre in Warsaw.
The regional hospital in Szczecin worked on paper after ransomware; the attackers reportedly demanded several million dollars. Hospitals in Kraków and Szczecin needed national emergency support.
The Eskulap medical centre in Racibórz: records encrypted, high risk that data was stolen.

The national e-health centre counts 13 ransomware incidents in health care so far in 2026 against 10 in all of 2025. A leak at a medical software platform covered close to 19 million people; investigators said in February 2026 they had identified who was behind it.

The judicial police confirmed that personal data of more than 100,000 users of the national health service was stolen. The attackers posed as a doctor; investigators say artificial intelligence may have been used. No suspect yet.
The national health insurer was targeted, in the same weeks as the attack that shut the land registry.

The health service of Extremadura detected on 5 October that its online health-centre app had been breached: clinical information of 18,416 users. Police arrested the suspected attacker in Mérida on 29 October.
Ransomware at the health foundation Radix: data stolen and encrypted, including data of the federal administration, one of its clients.
Two medical centres in Chur confirmed that patient data, including prescriptions and X-rays, was taken; the Cloak group claims 87 GB.
After the drone reports Denmark banned all civilian drone flights for the days when European leaders met in Copenhagen.

The army's Cyber Command has about 300 people. Behind it stands the cyber unit of the volunteer Defence League, staffed by IT professionals; in wartime the command would grow to about four times its size from that pool. A separate civilian cyber reserve of the state IT authority has held five exercises with operators of vital services, the latest at Tallinn Airport.
Estonia spends an estimated 5.1% of its economy on core defence.
Finland and Poland announced that they will jointly lead the EU project to guard the eastern border (Eastern Flank Watch).

A break-in at the phone-management service of the state IT centre Valtori reportedly exposed data on military officers, diplomats and counter-terrorism staff; police widened the investigation in April.
The army is building a Cyber Defence Regiment that will reach 400 people from the three services by 2030, next to its cyber command.
Parliament passed a law letting approved operators of vital infrastructure and their contractors detect, jam and shoot down drones near designated sites. Reported in October 2026.
An estimated 2.22% of the economy on core defence.
The Cyber and Information Domain Service, a full branch of the armed forces, counted 15,659 people.

Parliament changed the aviation security law: the armed forces may jam or shoot down drones when a state asks for help, and the defence ministry decides alone. Flying a drone into an airport's security zone became a crime.
An estimated 2.69% of the economy on core defence.
A high-ranking military officer was arrested on espionage charges; for whom is not stated in the reports found.

Reuters reported that Russia-linked hackers broke into 27 email accounts of the Hellenic National Defence General Staff, part of a wider campaign whose main target was Ukraine. The General Staff did not answer questions. Less established outlets name the Russian military-intelligence group APT28.
An estimated 3.65% of the economy on core defence.
A proposal for a national military cyber body: 1,200 to 1,500 people at first, growing to 5,000 including reservists. An estimated 2.1% of the economy on core defence.
An estimated 4.92% of the economy on core defence. The July 2026 draft drew a record 1,560 volunteers; the aim is 4,000 conscripts a year by 2028.

The highest spender in NATO: an estimated 5.33% of the economy on core defence. 5,000 conscripts are called up for 2026, with new cyber training. Lithuania is named among the countries that passed a law on bringing down drones; no details found. It has no civilian volunteer cyber reserve.

The defence cyber strategy of 2025 treats cyber as a military domain in its own right; a defence cyber academy is being set up and recruitment for the cyber command is a priority. The Netherlands commits to NATO's 3.5% for core defence only, not to the extra 1.5%.
Norway takes part in the EU's Eastern Flank Watch and commits to the 3.5% for core defence only.
About 6,500 people in the Cyberspace Defence Forces, with defensive, reconnaissance and offensive tasks, plus a reserve called the Cyber Legion of around 3,000 (ministry, February 2026).
An estimated 4.68% of the economy on core defence. Poland co-leads Eastern Flank Watch and says it wants a working drone wall within three months, a national timetable.
An estimated 2.1% of the economy on core defence. Nothing specific on cyber forces found.
The president signed a law allowing troops to shoot down drones in Romanian airspace. Date taken from a headline.
The Joint Cyberspace Command presented a growth plan: 1,500 people by 2030, three times its present strength.
a record 756 attacks to knock Estonian websites offline, more than a third above 2024; fewer than a hundred had any effect (state information system authority RIA).
criminals encrypted the patient data, medical records and appointments of a family medicine centre (RIA).
NoName057(16) attacked Finnish websites, without significant effect (Traficom).
the highest number of registered cyber threats ever; Russia is named as the main source (state security service).
the laboratory Clinical Diagnostics, which analyses cervical-cancer screening: data of more than 405,000 women stolen. The health inspectorate found it had not met legal security standards.
the national health insurer VšZP was targeted in a separate attack.
bpost: Ransomware. Core operations not disrupted.
Héron (municipality): Servers unreachable; accounting and planning services stopped for days. No ransom paid.

ransomware shut the national land registry (ÚGKK). Offices closed, property transactions were suspended, and even parking permits in Bratislava stopped. The minister called it the largest cyberattack in the country's history; most services returned by March.
the airline Iberia confirmed that customers' names, emails, phone numbers and loyalty-card numbers were reached.
Supreme Administrative Court: a large part of its computer systems was affected and part of the work moved to manual procedures.
the RansomHub group claimed 180 GB from the National Archaeological Institute of the National Museum.
The Bulgarian branch of insurer Uniqa was hit by ransomware with a demand of about €6 million.
Port of Ostend: Cyberattack on the port.
A pro-Russian group attacked about 20 Italian websites, including major banks and airports, for several days. No significant disruption (national cyber agency).
ransomware completely disrupted the systems of EETAA, the agency that supports local government.
Local authorities, provinces, federal departments: CCB advisory: repeated DDoS made public websites unavailable.
The Interior Ministry hospital in Kraków: ransomware encrypted files and the hospital lost access to some systems.
A breach at Pharmadata, an IT supplier to pharmacies, was described by the national cyber centre as the most serious incident of the period.
The Bonifraterskie Medical Centre in Warsaw: ransomware encrypted data on its servers.
The network of a joint municipal authority (not named) was infected with malware that affected its information systems.

Hackers opened a valve of a dam at Bremanger and let 500 litres of water per second flow for about four hours before it was noticed. No damage. In August 2025 Norway's security service blamed pro-Russian hackers, the first time Oslo formally pointed at Moscow for a cyberattack.
Jemeppe-sur-Sambre (municipality): Servers down. Attackers demanded €700,000.

A group linked to Russian intelligence targeted a heating plant in western Sweden; the plant's security systems stopped the attack (Minister for Civil Defence). Norway and Denmark saw similar attempts.
Walloon Public Service (SPW): Intrusion: all internet links cut. Legal deadlines extended by 60 days, later 150 days, by decree.
CPAS Rebecq: Ransomware.

hackers got into the control systems of five water treatment plants (Jabłonna Lacka, Szczytno, Małdyty, Tolkmicko, Sierakowo) and could change settings; factory passwords played a part. One city nearly lost its water in August 2025 (security agency ABW).
State Security (VSSE), phones: Ivanti mobile-management software at an external partner exploited. Staff names, phone numbers and emails possibly stolen. Disclosed 20 Jun 2026.
the government formally blamed China's state-linked group APT31 for a campaign running since 2022 against an unclassified network of the Foreign Ministry, and summoned the Chinese ambassador.
parking.brussels: Unauthorised access to systems.
Russian-linked hackers broke into at least four mailboxes of local officials in the Plovdiv region.
Roularta Media Group: DDoS disrupted websites, apps and printing.
Ransomware at the health foundation Radix: data was stolen and encrypted, including data of the federal administration, which is one of its clients.
Hackers claimed about 41 GB of passenger data from Cyprus Airways; the airline neither confirmed nor denied it.
A cinema company active in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania: ransomware encrypted all its virtual servers and its backups; recovery took a long time, but the cinemas stayed open.
the Nova group claimed the Faculty of Science of the University of Zagreb.
Orange Belgium: 850,000 customer accounts. Names, numbers, SIM IDs and PUK codes exposed, which enables SIM-swap fraud.
Dry-cleaning chain 5àsec was hit by ransomware; data was stolen to put pressure on the company.
The Ameos hospital group shut down all its systems after an attack; several German states opened data-protection proceedings.
The employment agency France Travail: data of about 340,000 job seekers reached through a partner's application.

the Public Prosecution Service took all its systems offline after a break-in through Citrix remote-access software. It caused a backlog of about 9,000 cases; a committee found in October 2026 that security had fallen short for years.

an attack on POST Luxembourg cut landlines, mobile phones and access to the emergency number 112 for more than three hours. The government called it targeted; in May 2026 POST said it used an unpublished flaw in Huawei network routers.

ransomware at Miljödata, a supplier of personnel software, disrupted about 200 of Sweden's 290 municipalities. The ransom asked was 1.5 bitcoin; data on more than a million people was published on 14 Sep 2025.
Bouygues Telecom: personal data of 6.4 million customer accounts, including bank account numbers.
A payroll service provider was the target of a targeted attack (Interior Ministry cybersecurity report for 2025).
Supermarket chain Auchan: data of a few hundred thousand loyalty-card customers.
Interior Ministry: unauthorised access to about 100 of its 60,000 email accounts.
Public hospitals in the Hauts-de-France region were targeted through the servers that hold patients' identity data.
Brussels Airport, via Collins Aerospace: Ransomware on MUSE check-in software. About half of departures cancelled on day one, disruption until 28 Sep. UK NCA arrested a man in his 40s.
Berlin Brandenburg Airport: check-in and baggage systems down for days after ransomware at the supplier Collins Aerospace, the same attack that hit Brussels Airport.
an attack took the tax service, the national portal Latvija.lv and the government website offline for about an hour.
Military bases and airports: Drone swarms over Marche-en-Famenne and Kleine Brogel; Brussels and Liège airspace closed. Francken: "hybrid war".

Cyprus Post confirmed a cyberattack; screenshots of mail addressed to the Presidential Palace, ministries and embassies appeared on the dark web. The post office says the central database was not reached.
Furniture chain Poltronesofà: ransomware with possible theft and encryption of data.
Telecom, health and intelligence websites: Two related NoName057(16) DDoS campaigns.
The RansomHouse group claimed the textile maker Fulgar; on 8 November the DragonForce group claimed the firm Ponzini.
The city of Ludwigshafen took all its IT offline; an external attack was later confirmed.
The RansomHouse group claimed the construction firm Polidano Group.
Climbing-wall maker Walltopia was hit by ransomware.
the solar contractor Solarpro Holding appeared on a ransomware leak site.
the Interior Ministry confirmed that hackers reached email servers and a limited number of confidential files, including parts of police record systems.
ransomware in the business systems of the Oltenia Energy Complex, which produces about 30% of Romania's electricity. The power system stayed stable.
Provinces and municipalities: NoName057(16) campaign: Belgium accounted for 57.3% of all attack entries across 15+ countries.
The youth employment network Missions Locales: data of about 1.6 million young people exposed.
The regional government of Mazovia: its electronic document system was encrypted, and more than 300 local authorities lost access and had to disconnect.
Germany formally blamed Russia's military-intelligence hackers (APT28) for an August 2024 attack on its air traffic control company, and summoned the Russian ambassador.
A breach of the Grund care home's systems exposed data on tens of thousands of people; disclosed in February 2026. Iceland's cyber team, Europol and Interpol investigate.

Danish military intelligence blamed a pro-Russian group (Z-Pentest) for a destructive attack on a water utility near Køge in 2024 that left about 50 households without water for hours, and another (NoName057(16)) for attacks on websites before the November 2025 local elections. It linked both groups to the Russian state; the ambassador was summoned.
ransomware at the national water authority Apele Române: about 1,000 computers and 10 of its 11 regional offices. The attackers used Windows' own encryption tool.
Food company Fiorucci was hit by ransomware over the Christmas period, disrupting orders.

a destructive attack on about 30 energy sites (heat-and-power plants, wind and solar). It failed, but could have cut power to 500,000 people. On 13 Jul 2026 the EU and UK attributed it to Russia's FSB Centre 16 and imposed their first coordinated cyber sanctions.
a telecom cable of operator Elisa in the Gulf of Finland was damaged; police seized the cargo ship Fitburg. Traffic was rerouted. Physical sabotage, not a hack.
The company building the Brenner Base Tunnel confirmed that outsiders reached part of its data that was accessible over the internet. The Everest group claims 812 GB; that figure is not confirmed.
Casinos Austria: online-shop data of about 150,000 customers reached through an external service provider; no bank or card data.
Health software company Cegedim Santé: the health minister confirmed the attack could concern more than 15 million people.
The Ministry of Ecological Transition confirmed a cyberattack; the Anubis group claims more than 22,000 records.
The association of French mayors: more than 100,000 records taken, including passwords stored in clear text.
The website of Nyköping municipality was manipulated by unknown attackers; the municipality said the problem was isolated.
Zermatt Tourism confirmed a cyberattack in which customer data may have been taken.
At least four large private health facilities in Milan and Rome were hit by ransomware with extortion demands (not named).
The World Leaks group claims about 8.5 terabytes from the media company Mediaworks Hungary and threatened to publish it.
an attack that flooded a Cypriot bank's systems lasted about 200 hours, more than eight days: longer than any attack the security firm Qrator Labs recorded in 2025.
the Czech cyber agency reported that Russia's military-intelligence hackers (APT28) took over internet routers in Czechia through a known flaw and unchanged factory passwords, to intercept logins.
Finnair customer data was caught in a breach at booking supplier Amadeus; ferry company Viking Line reported a breach of a pre-order system.
the Prime Minister reportedly said France has recorded about three data thefts a day since the start of the year.
the gift company Smartbox Group reported unauthorised access to a platform holding customers' names and email addresses.

more than 600,000 entries were taken from the national registers of property and companies, using the logins of institutions that were allowed to consult them. The head of the Centre of Registers resigned; prosecutors suspect a foreign state.
hospitals in Kraków and Szczecin needed national emergency support.
trackers list the paper maker The Navigator Company (Mar), the municipality of Serpa (May) and the University of Aveiro (Jul) as ransomware victims.
probable ransomware at gas supplier Geoplin, with limited effect (CERT-EU); in June the Sinobi group claimed it and demanded $8.2 million.
the energy company Endesa confirmed a breach of customer data, including identity and bank-account numbers. The attacker claims 20 million people; Endesa has about 10 million customers.
incidents reported at the Port of Vigo and the supermarket chain Ahorramás (Qilin ransomware).
